speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DUMPING-REFERENCE TO ACTION TAKEN BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the last sitting the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked the following questions:
1. Has the government given consideration to the new regulations issued by the United States treasury with respect to the establishment of fair value on imports in relation to dumping, and also to the bill that was produced in congress last month on the same subject?
I will answer this question first. The answer is that the Department of Trade and Commerce has carefully studied the new regulations published by the United States treasury department on April 12, 1955, to introduce certain changes into the administration of the United States anti-dumping legislation. While they will not make a great deal

Inquiries of the Ministry of difference, the amendments may be regarded as helpful to our exporters. The regulations have been simplified and some elements of uncertainty have been removed. For anti-dumping purposes, recognition is given to the fact that it is normal business practice to have different prices for different classes of customers. In other words, in pricing goods for export a trader will be able to apply the same price structure as he uses in domestic sales without fear of running afoul of the United States anti-dumping laws. Until these new regulations have been in force for a period of time it will, of course, not be possible to know precisely what effect they may have on trade. The government is not aware that any legislation is before congress to amend the United States anti-dumping laws.
The second question is:
Is the government satisfied that these measures do not contravene the provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade?
The answer is: It would not appear that there is any necessary conflict between these new regulations and the relevant provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
The third question is:
If the government is of the opinion that they do, what action is the government taking in the direction of making representations in regard to either the regulations or the bill before congress?
The answer is that we are not of the opinion that they do.

maintopic: DUMPING-REFERENCE TO ACTION TAKEN BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: I wonder whether the minister can expand somewhat on his answer respecting the legislation as distinct from the regulations. The article in Foreign Trade to which I drew the minister's attention yesterday did make mention of the fact that a bill had been introduced in congress on May 5. The minister's statement indicates that the department was not aware of any legislation being introduced. Can the minister expand on his answer in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DUMPING-REFERENCE TO ACTION TAKEN BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: This question has reference to legislation against dumping, and my officers are not aware that any bill is being introduced affecting dumping. There is the customs simplification bill which has passed the appropriate committee, I believe yesterday, and which we hope will be approved by congress before it adjourns. However, that does not affect dumping, and as I read my hon. friend's question it applied only to dumping legislation.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 481, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
Mr. Speaker, I did not know that it was the Prairie Farm Assistance Act that was being called. I had one or two words to say about it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Apparently the hon. member was caught by surprise, but the second reading has already been pronounced and I was putting the motion for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole. I do not think the hon. member will be prejudiced because he can make the representations he wishes to make on clause 1, in committee. Perhaps we were a little hasty in our proceedings but, since this was announced last night and has been on the order paper for some time, we thought that perhaps hon. members were agreeable to let the second reading go by. Is it agreed that I now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on this bill?

Agreed.
The house in committee on Bill No. 481, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Cultivated land.

Things were going so fast a few moments ago that I missed out. It is unusual in this house for things to go quite with that celerity. I can say now what I intended to say a few moments ago. As far as the amendments in question are concerned, they do in general cover the unusual conditions resulting this year and last year from a larger amount of moisture than in living memory. I would, however, like to make one or two general observations.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
The necessity for the clause that removes the need of contiguous sections has been established. Indeed, in many cases this year farmers have been denied prairie farm assistance payments while a neighbour across the line or in the next section is receiving it. That discrimination has created a very considerable amount of ill feeling. This amendment is the major one, as I see it, and will go a long way to meet that criticism.
I have one suggestion to make to the minister in this connection, in view of existing circumstances, which could not have been anticipated. As a rule, I am very much opposed to anything in the nature of retroactive legislation, but may I ask whether consideration has been given to this new definition as provided for by the amendment being applicable this year in such a way as to cover the farmers who are now denied the payment in respect of the 1954 crop? I do not think it would be a very costly matter. It would not be a serious invasion of the rule that is usually applied, that retroactive legislation should not be passed, but it would meet a situation that is particularly grievous this year.
In so far as the other clauses are concerned, which provide for amending the definition of cultivated lands, and which will enable payments to be made on those lands that have been flooded, I think that these amendments are worthy of commendation and of unqualified support. However, I ask the minister this question. In order to cover the situation thoroughly, for instance, should not paragraph (d) (ii) of subsection 1 of section 2 of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be altered in one particular? It reads as follows:
(d) "cultivated land" means land that in the year of award was seeded to crop or was In summerfallow and includes . . .
(ii) land of a farmer that in three out of the five years immediately preceding the year of award had been seeded or summerfallowed, but owing to natural causes beyond his control could not be seeded or summerfallowed in the year of award:
Is it necessary or does it not reduce the ambit of this legislation to have the second "summerfallowed" inserted? In other words, should the last line not read "beyond his control could not be seeded in the year of award"? It is difficult to imagine a situation, regardless of flood conditions, where some degree of summerfallowing could not be done. I bring that matter to the attention of the minister and ask him whether he has given consideration to that portion of the section which, in my opinion, may work a hardship on those who are intended to be entitled.
A similar representation would also apply
in the other portions of the amendment in

Prairie Farm Assistance Act which the word "summerfallowed" is mentioned. If it should refer to summerfallowing at all, should it not say "in whole or in part"? I ask this because the question as to when a piece of land has been summerfallowed has been productive of a great deal of litigation over the years. When is summerfallowing completed? Unless the words "in whole or in part" are inserted after the word "summerfallowed" I can see that, on a strict interpretation of the qualifying sections and the amending sections, many could conceivably be denied any entitlement.
I think those are the only observations I have to make. I feel that these amendments are necessary in that they cover a situation which has become apparent in the last few years. My only suggestions, in order to make the amendments more workable, are those that I have placed before the minister. One is to make the general section 3 retroactive in order to cover the situation that we have today in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba; and the second is to add after the word "summerfallowed" the words "in whole or in part" in order to cover the situation arising out of the amount of litigation as to the meaning of the word "summerfallowed" which has indicated the need for those words being added.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not of course refer to section 3 until we get to it, but I think the same argument applies to section 1 in connection with the matter of whether or not the bill is retroactive. In reading the main act it will be found that the year under this act is from August 1 until July 31. There are almost six weeks left in this year. Any adjustments which are required to be made would be made before August 1 in any case. I think there is authority in the bill. As a matter of fact my understanding of the case is that it is retroactive to that extent.
Coming to the suggestion that was made, we did give consideration to the idea that has been expressed, and it was the thought of the draftsmen that the section as it reads, taken together with the administration of the act over the years, does mean what my hon. friend is suggesting even as the wording is now. It reads:
. . . land of a farmer that in three out of the five years immediately preceding the year of award had been seeded or summerfallowed-
I understand there is no objection to that. That is clear.
-but owing to natural causes beyond his control could not be seeded or summerfallowed in the year of award.
That is the one.

I think in effect that part of it would be applied in much the same way as the words used by the hon. member for Prince Albert suggest. I do not think there would be any change. There certainly would not be any change in the administration. We have been accustomed to taking the word of farmers and their neighbours as to what they intended to do with the land or what had been done with it and then arrive at a conclusion whether or not the man did intend to summerfallow the land. It is pretty difficult to go beyond that.
A very considerable part of the payments made this year have been made on lands that could not be properly seeded in the year gone by, but when an attempt had been made to summerfallow. There was no difficulty about that. The difficulty was in connection with land that was not seeded or summerfallowed last year at all because it was flooded or there was some other reason they could not get on the land at the right time to do the work. It is possible now to make payments if the land was not seeded last year and not seeded this year because of conditions over which the farmer had no control if it had been seeded and/or summer-fallowed in three of the last five years. I think it is necessary to have it as broad as it is in order to make the necessary payments.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some comment on the amendment to the act now before us. I am quite sure western farmers will welcome the change making some provision for land which cannot be seeded because of flood conditions. I am sure it will be of some assistance to them, but I should like to point out to the committee that the maximum awards made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act of $250 in areas eligible on the basis of $1,50 an acre and $500 in areas eligible on the basis of $2.50 an acre are very small amounts of money so far as compensation for crop loss is concerned. When one considers western farmers' costs of operation today and the fact that a load of fuel will probably use up $200 or $300, one can readily understand that the P.F.A.A. awards as now made do not in any way compensate for crop loss in western Canada.
However, we favour any adjustment which will make payments possible to farmers who, through no fault of their own, are losing the opportunity to get revenue from their land. I should like to point out that in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 16, 1955, there is a comment to the effect that the Minister of Agriculture had stated that in the last 16 years farmers had paid, through deductions on the sale of their grain, more than they

had received from the fund. That is a fact, and no one should look upon these payments as being a subsidy to western farmers. They have paid into the fund over the years. It is true that when conditions are such that they lose their crop they receive some compensation.
I should also like to point out that there are many types of farmers who are not covered by the present legislation. I should like to direct the committee's attention again to the Winnipeg Free Press article of June 16 entitled, "Embittered Cattlemen Miss Help." This article points out that the livestock producer receives no compensation for crop loss under the present bill. Inasmuch as the grain farmer does get compensation, they are taking strong exception to the act as at present constituted.

I should like to ask the hon. member a question, because he comes from an area in which there is considerable livestock. The fact is the very opposite to what the hon. member says. I think he will recognize that the livestock producer does not pay anything on livestock, but he is paid even if all his grain is fed.

The
fact is that that is not always so.
It is always the case.

So the
article is quite true; and the attitude of the cattlemen to the act holds good.
The greatest objection to the amendment being made is with respect to the change in the section which will make provision for going back to the rectangular block in making awards, or for taking areas out. I feel that this amendment, as it appears in the bill, is a retrograde movement, and will bring us back to the position we occupied formerly when the act was constituted on a rectangular basis.
I think it was a concession to the farmer when the government agreed to bring in an award made on the basis of a block of contiguous sections. I fully realize that there might be some injustice in the way in which the act is now constituted, but-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, may I point out that we have not yet reached clause 3 in the bill. Because the hon. member for Prince Albert was not present during the debate on second reading he was permitted to discuss clause 3 or to say something about its application. However, Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to insist upon a discussion of the clause now before the committee.
50433-319i
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
I have been making a general statement, and have not been referring specifically to any clause.
I suggest my hon. friend should have made this speech on second reading. If he desires to make it, he may do so when we reach clause 3; but I am not prepared to discuss it at the moment.

wish to say is that we in this group favour the change by which the farmer who loses his crop owing to flood conditions, or for any other reason, is covered. It is well understood that the act was drawn up in the first instance to compensate farmers for loss of crops due mainly to drought. The present extension of the act will give coverage to those farmers who lose their crops for any other reason, and I favour that provision.
But, as I say, when we come to the clause which makes provision for going back to the rectangular block we in this group intend to oppose the amendment so that it will continue on the present basis.

Mr. Chairman, I think there will be general satisfaction over the proposal to make payment on land that cannot be seeded. The original purpose of the act was to deal with drought conditions, but during the past few years the farmers have suffered heavy loss as a result of flooding. It is only logical that land that is flooded early in the season and hence cannot be seeded should be eligible for payment under the act.
While I say this about that particular proposal, I do not believe there will be the same amount of enthusiasm displayed in regard to the amendment which would have the effect of reverting to the rectangular block. However, I shall leave what I wish to say on that point until we reach clause 3, because I think there are two sides even to that question.
However, in dealing with the general subject matter of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act I find a lot of dissatisfaction throughout the country, especially in areas where payments are made continuously and in areas where payments are made only once in a while, over the fact that the farmers are compelled to contribute to this scheme without receiving any guarantee that, in the event of crop failure, they will receive any assistance.
For a number of years the farmers have been asking that losses should be assessed on an individual basis, and that is the reason why from time to time amendments have been made to the act reducing the size of the basic area. It is interesting to note that today all farm organizations are asking the

Prairie Farm Assistance Act government to bring in a system of crop insurance. This was advocated by the federation of agriculture in their brief to the government; it was advocated by the western pools and also by the farm unions.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been in operation since 1939, so up to this time the government must have built up a pretty complete record of the productivity of the land in western Canada. Having that information, it would be a quite simple matter for the government to zone the areas in the west, based upon the productivity of the land, so that the districts could be adjusted in accordance with crops in areas over a period of time. Votes could be taken in each of those districts as to whether or not the farmers would like to continue under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, or come in under a crop insurance scheme.
If this were done I do not think any hardship would be created in areas where crop losses occur continuously. The farmers there would vote to continue under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act because, obviously, if their losses were occurring continuously their premiums under a system of crop insurance would be prohibitive. Therefore they would continue under the act. On the other hand, where crop failures occurred only occasionally farmers would prefer to pay higher premiums and be covered against loss under a system of crop insurance so that, in the event of loss, they would receive compensation. Of course under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act there can be no guarantee that in the event of loss a farmer will receive compensation, because the determining factor is the way the land in the surrounding area has been affected. If other land has also suffered crop failure there is a good chance that the farmer will receive assistance; but if the other land has not been affected that farmer would not be likely to receive that assistance under the act.
In view of the fact that crop insurance has been in operation in the United States since 1938, I suggest the government could learn a great deal from the experience that has been gained in that country. It is true that in the early years heavy losses were suffered under their act; but for the last six years in the United States premiums and indemnities have balanced-and that in spite of the fact that they have had three years of heavy crop failures.
So in view of the fact that over a period of time the government must have been able to build up a record of the productivity of land in western Canada, and in view of the further fact that the United States has gained a lot
[Mr. Quelch l
of experience in the operation of crop insurance, I suggest the government would be well advised to work in co-operation with the provinces with a view to setting up a system of crop insurance.
I know that in the past the minister has argued that a system of all-risk crop insurance would be ultra vires. It seems to me that if a scheme were brought in on a voluntary basis there would be no question as to the government's not having power. Just as hail insurance companies can write hail insurance in a province, I do not see why we cannot have a national all-risk crop insurance scheme on a voluntary basis.
Even so, if the minister is right when he says that the government would not have the constitutional powers required, there would be nothing to prevent this government passing a national crop insurance act, and then each province passing enabling legislation to come in under such act, as we do in connection with marketing legislation. I hope the minister will give us some assurance that this matter is being considered, especially in light of the fact that all farm organizations today are asking that such action be taken. I want to say a word on clause 3, but I shall wait until we come to it.

I want to say a general word on Bill No. 481. I wish to commend the minister particularly for the first part of the bill. The bill is made up of two parts. We all know from experience of the last years that the unseeded land has always been a problem when it came to ascertaining the average yield in a township. Quite often it worked against the rest of the land. To what extent it will be applicable in our province of Manitoba only time will tell. However, the principle is a good one and I am sure it will prove to be of some benefit.
I do not intend to refer to any specific clauses of the bill at this stage. However, I should like to say that when we amended the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in 1949 the major amendments were made at that time. We included in the act provisions for river lots. Up until that time river lots were not able to qualify under the act because they were not constituted as a township. The act mentioned only a regular township as surveyed by the dominion survey. We did provide in the definition that a group of river lots could be constituted into a township by the governor in council. However, we did not tidy up the rest of the act and experience has shown that the river lot townships have been applicable only under section 3. Most of the other sections of the act have not applied to the river lot townships. While we

are dealing with this amendment I am going to suggest when we come to the appropriate clause of this bill, that we include the block settlement and river lots that have been constituted into a regular township and so defined by the act. I am going to suggest that they come under, particularly, section 6 because section 6 is by far the most important section of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. When we come to that particular section I shall deal with the question further but I would appreciate it very much-

May I
ask the hon. member a question? Does the phrase "river lots" appear in the regulations or in the bill?

"River lots" appears in the definition of the bill. If the hon. member will read the definition of township as contained in the act he will find that townships are defined as follows:
"Township" means, in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, a township according to the system of survey authorized by the Dominion Land Surveys Act, chapter 117 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, and in the province of British Columbia a township whose boundaries are confirmed by the official surveys act of British Columbia.
This was added in 1949:
and includes any group of settlements or river lots declared by the governor in council to be a township for the purposes of this act.
Therefore, in effect, these are what we commonly refer to as block townships or block river lots. As far as the act is concerned, they are just as much townships as the regular surveyed townships. But the wording in other sections refers to sections, and there are no sections in the river lots, and consequently application has proved almost impossible.

It has always been my conception of a debate on the first clause that it was pretty general. We were allowed to discuss almost any clause of a bill in the broad sense. This morning the minister tried to keep the discussion strictly to the first clause. That is not my idea of the discussion on the first clause. It has always been of a pretty general nature.
I should like to add a further word to what the hon. member for Prince Albert said on clause 1 (d) (ii). Can the minister say what would happen, for instance, where a man had intended to seed the acreage but the land was flooded and was so wet that he could not get on it until July? Then it dried up sufficiently so that he could summer-fallow. Is it the intention of this bill to disallow any payment because of the fact that he could summerfallow? That would be perfectly justifiable under the wording of
Prairie Farm Assistance Act this legislation because, had he intended to seed and did not seed, he could be paid. Summerfallow is mentioned in the wording of this bill. If he could summerfallow later on in the season, then he could be disqualified under the present wording.
I can understand that the minister wants this in the bill as protection for himself and his officials in the event that the man intended to summerfallow all the time. In view of the fact that summerfallowing was not carried through he might be paid as though he intended to seed. Does the minister follow me? I think the word "summerfallow" might be a deterrent to some farmers who had intended to seed.

If I might answer now, that is exactly the point which is involved. Seeding is usually completed by June 10. This year it has carried on to that and a little beyond it. Summerfallowing, if it is done well, is done in June. Sometimes it is done up until the middle of July; but if a person simply withholds from summerfallowing because he wants to draw under this act the inspector has the right to turn him down. He is supposed to go on farming as though this act did not exist. If he finds it is possible to summerfallow in June, and he does not, well, he should not be allowed to draw under the act on account of that. It is only where it is proven that it is absolutely impossible for him either to have seeded or to have summerfallowed right through until, if you like, the middle of July; there would be some date that the inspector would have in his mind in each of the different districts as to when payment would be made.
Summerfallowing is done earlier in Manitoba, for example, than it is up in the Peace river area, but the date will have to be pretty well established in the minds of the inspectors when they are checking as to whether the farmer really farmed when he could have farmed; and if it was not possible for him to farm because of natural conditions over which he had no control, payment would be possible; but if he simply avoided summerfallowing for the purpose of getting under this legislation he would not be paid.

What about the other chap who intended to seed but found that the end of June was too late for him to do the seeding that he had planned, but he summer-fallowed? Would he be deprived of the payment under the legislation even though he had intended to seed the land?

In most cases that land would come into next year's payment, because if he summerfallows it then he will seed it the next year or he may seed to rye that

Prairie Farm Assistance Act year. It is a quite common practice in the west to seed rye in August on summerfallow, and that could be done. He draws on that particular crop if the conditions the next year are such that he should draw on it; but it is not intended to give him any inducements whatsoever to cease to farm in order to get under this legislation. He is supposed to farm in the way he would have farmed if the act had never been there.

In the past, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act had to do with drought districts. It is probably quite fair that the flooded areas should be brought under the act. I am not arguing against that. I do want to say this, however. It has been said that a crop insurance plan should be brought in. The hon. member for Acadia did not mention the eastern part of Canada. I think something can be said for this act or a similar act being applied to eastern Canada as well as to western Canada. Last fall thousands of acres could not be harvested because of flood conditions following "Hurricane Hazel".
When I spoke on the first item of the agriculture estimates I suggested that the scheme could be applied to all of Canada, not merely western Canada.

I do not remember that having been said, but I do feel it is unfair when a farmer in eastern Canada for reasons beyond his control cannot harvest a crop he has seeded because of flood conditions. I think these farmers have a proper beef. If any consideration is to be given to a crop insurance scheme it should cover the whole of Canada, not just the four western provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join the hon. member for Provencher in congratulating the minister upon the amendments he has brought in. In eastern Manitoba we find a great difference in the districts. The levels will vary and crop conditions differ generally from section to section. The reduction of the area to six sections in the case of flooding will certainly be of assistance. The Manitoba government set up a crop insurance commission which brought in an interim report on March 25, 1955, in which they indicated that the main dissatisfaction with P.F.A.A. was as follows.
First, the payments are too small. Second, disproportionate amounts have been collected and paid out in Manitoba because this province enjoys relatively stable yields and does not, generally speaking, suffer the crop damage experienced further west.

Third, the act frequently fails to cover losses from flooding, insect damage, hail and other crop hazards which are typically local in nature. Fourth, the P.F.A.A. was designed primarily for drought, which is not Manitoba's main crop hazard. Fifth, the act is too inflexible. The 18-section block used as the basis of qualification is too large and too rigid.
Then they go on, and the twelfth item is that the act does not make any provision for land which owing to adverse spring conditions cannot be seeded.
Those were the suggestions received by this commission during its travels throughout the province. It has been suggested that there should be greater flexibility in the granting of benefits through a reduction in the size of the qualifying -block. I feel that in connection with flood damage the present provision for 6-section blocks will prove a partial answer, if not the whole answer to these complaints which were expressed by people who came before that commission. I thought in all fairness that these should be put on the record.

Mr. Chairman, I want to congratulate the minister upon bringing in amendments to this act. Just how far they will go toward meeting the difficulties being experienced in my own province is something I shall have to wait to see. But it is nice to know that something is being done about it. I shall try to keep my remarks as general as possible and not touch upon specific clauses in the bill, but I am worrying over not seeing anything in the bill which will help the fellow who bought land from the government after 1940. He will not be able to participate in any scheme which the minister brings along.
The hon. member for Provencher referred to the river lot business. There is a lot of dissatisfaction about these river lots and the way they are rounded up. I hope the minister will take this into consideration.
I believe the minister is doing something worth while when he is taking into consideration flooded land which prevents people from sowing crops. I do not know whether this provision should be permanently in the act, but at the present time there are many people close to starvation who have no crops or anything. Something will have to be done for them.
Farmers up in the interlake country do not generally grow grain outside of what is required for their cattle. I have a letter here from one farmer who states:
They tell us they'll pay us flood relief but this is based on wheat land. We are not grain farmers,

none of us; we are mixed farmers. I have 90 sheep, 4 horses, 19 head of cattle grazing on about a 30-acre knoll.
That is all he has.
We try to grow enough for our chickens and stock with perhaps 100 to 1,000 bushels to sell.
These people milk their cows all summer. I do not know of anything in this act that will help them. Another man writes and tells me that his son has got into the habit of swimming every night for the cows. That may seem an absurd statement to make in the House of Commons, but it is true.
Do the cows swim back?

I am surprised at my hon. friend doubting my word. If cows get up on a knoll they will stay there until you go to get them and I think my hon. friend realizes that. That is a terrible position to be in.
I know a farmer who has been swimming his cows back and forth across a river all summer.

Maybe they have got to like it, but these fellows have not been acclimatized as yet. It is an innovation to them and they have not got the cows trained to swim. Another lady writes to me saying that she has had to build a raft in order to do her chores. When people are inundated with water to that extent, what chance have they of making a living or getting anywhere?
Then there is the problem, which I have referred to the Minister of Agriculture many times, of the man on one side of a road getting nothing while his neighbour across the road gets a benefit payment. This bill is to change the system back to the one we had in the early stages. I do not know whether it is going to help and the minister's officers who have been out in the field may know whether it is going to remedy that situation. The fact is that quite often a man on one side of the road gets nothing while his neighbour across the road may get a payment of $150. I know the minister will answer that a line must be drawn somewhere. But I am afraid the line is being drawn too quickly. We have to find some way to break that down. I was going to say something about the rectangular blocks, but I know it will be ruled out of order and I shall refrain from doing so.
In the interlake country the men are leaving the farms. That is not good for agriculture, it is not good for the country. A year ago the people who had a crop found that it was polluted with worms and rust. Only the individual who was able to get a few bushels of Selkirk wheat had any crop. They have nothing to go on. I have had
Prairie Farm Assistance Act some of the most deplorable letters I have ever come across. One says:
I have been drowned out for two years. This is the third. Definitely no crop whatever this year. Now those who do not raise grain have been paid $200 for only 25 acres, and in three or four cases near here there has not been any land cleared; and some have been retired for seven to 10 years, yet they receive $200. In my case, with absolutely no crop for two years and none this year and with 98 acres under cultivation, I received $72, while my neighbour with 18 acres gets $150.
These are things that should be straightened out. Then there are the individuals who cannot come under P.F.A.A. They will be just as hungry as the other ones. I do not know what we are going to do unless the minister brings in some other scheme to protect them or extends the benefits of P.F.A.A. to everyone in that area. They are very hard up, and I do not know how they are going to get through the next winter. When the minister speaks, I should like him to take a few minutes of his time to tell us about the man who is working in town and hires his work on the farm, or spends so many months in town and so many months on the farm. That is something the people across the dominion would like to have explained. I have heard myself of some cases and have been able to get them settled fairly satisfactorily, but I should like the minister to explain that when he answers. I do not wish to say any more. The minister knows the position in the interlake country. Everybody is drowned out. A good deal of money has been paid there, but it has not helped enough people there. In the case of one man about whom I have told you, he has a good deal of hay land, and the cattle cannot cross on it because it is flooded. It is 800 acres, and everything is under water. Surely there must be some relief that could be given to these people to help them to exist through this winter. I hope the minister will give these people consideration, that is, the people who cannot come under P.F.A.A. but who are just as badly off as those he has helped under P.F.A.A.

Like the hon. member for Acadia, I believe this bill is going to give some relief to some of the farmers throughout the west. However, there is one thing which was not mentioned here but which should be looked into carefully, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Acadia. That is some sort of revision in the act as far as hail damage is concerned. I have had literally dozens of letters from my own riding this year, some of them from people complaining that they had been hailed out for two or three years in succession. Although they have been paying into the fund

Prairie Farm Assistance Act every year, they cannot get any relief because of hail damage. They, of course, are blaming the officials and everybody in the department, but the fault is not with the officials. The fault lies in the act itself. The very way in which hail falls makes it impossible to make this act apply with any degree of equality.

Might I just say that there never was any intention under this bill to provide for hail damage. Hail damage insurance policies are provided by insurance companies and municipalities all over western Canada. A farmer can insure his crop against hail damage, but if incidentally he happens to be eligible under this act because the hail went across an area that comes under the act, than he is paid. But this act was never intended to provide hail insurance. That is provided by legislation in the three western provinces, and for the very same reason that I have given on many occasions as to why this government cannot bring in crop insurance. It was decided long ago in the last century after a good deal of discussion that the federal government could not put on hail insurance under the constitution. Therefore the three western provinces passed hail insurance bills. In the province of Saskatchewan the municipalities choose whether or not they come under it. The municipality where I live has always been under it. There one is insured to a limit of $5 an acre, and I usually put on another $5 an acre under a company. We have never come under the act in the municipality where I live until this year, but some have come in this year. The area I am in has not come in, but that is a possibility all the time. If that area is hailed out and it comes under the prairie farm assistance, the farmer gets paid. Areas that have never been under prairie farm assistance, of course, have not come in. There has never been any intention of hail coming under this at all, or anything else that the farmer himself can take care of. The farmer can insure his crop against hail at a very reasonable rate, and in view of that he is supposed to do so. If he does not, of course, the act does not protect him.

The minister is surely not suggesting that we have got ourselves into such a situation that the federal government and the provinces working together could not, if they so desired, put in a system of crop insurance.

What I am saying is that the government of Alberta, the government of Saskatchewan, or the government of Manitoba-they are three different parties, and

so I am not talking about one party-any one of those provinces, can bring in crop insurance and this government could assist after they have brought it in, if they felt inclined to do so, but the first action has to be taken by the provincial government. They have the authority to insure, and we have not. I may say that when this legislation was passed the province of Saskatchewan went very fully into the matter of insurance, and I have a summary of the report here before me. It was thought that at some time they would come in, but they never have. We are not criticizing them for that. That is their own decision. Apparently they think this legislation is fairly good and that nothing is necessary beyond that. But this is not something which we say to the provinces, "We have come into this, and you are not able to do anything about it". They were able to do all we have done, and they could add to it if they desired to add to it. If they do not desire to add to it, of course, we are not criticizing them.
Has the federal government intimated to the provinces that, if they did set up insurance, they would be given assistance by the federal government?

That is not the way that these things are done. If they say they are going to bring it in, it will then be a matter of saying whether this act should be supplemented or whether something else should be done. But they have not done so and I am quite satisfied that no government sitting here would try to work in that way.
The farm organizations have asked them to.

I can sympathize with what the minister has said and I can agree with him wholeheartedly that the act was not intended to cover hail. The fact remains that, now that it does cover hail, if the block is hailed and is declared eligible the farmers can collect under P.F.A.A. But it is disheartening to farmers to be hailed out year after year and to see their neighbours collecting from P.F.A.A. when they are not able to get anything because their area has been declared to be ineligible. That has happened on many occasions. I obtained a copy of a letter just recently that was sent to Mr. Rowbotham in Edmonton-

May I just clear up that point? I do not want to be misunderstood. These farmers would draw under P.F.A.A. It is not because of hail or because there was not any hail. They draw because that township is in under the act and whether they are hailed or whether they are not

hailed, they will draw; and they will draw the same amount as do their neighbours.

But the fact remains that these people who are in ineligible townships or blocks that have been declared to be ineligible are not collecting despite the fact that they have been paying into the fund for years. It is extremely disheartening.
As I was going to say when the minister interjected, I obtained a copy of a letter which was sent to Mr. Rowbotham's department in Edmonton complaining about the treatment they had received under P.F.A.A. It was signed by no less than 47 farmers in one area. That letter, coupled with dozens of complains that I have had, would indicate that there is a very large area in there which has been hailed out. As the minister knows, the hail travels in strips and it is impossible to make the act apply. If the minister is going to make the act apply to hail, I would urge that he change the act in such a way as to bring it down to a sectional basis or an individual basis, or change it in some way so that these people who have been paying into this fund for years can collect when they are hailed out.
There is one more thing to which I should like to refer. In the western part of my riding there is an area which was declared to be outside the act because it was considered to be a submarginal area. I realize that it was declared to be submarginal by the combined departments of agriculture of the federal government and the provincial government. However, since that time it has been discovered that certain crops grow well in that area. A good deal of clover is grown as well as alfalfa, and a good deal of success has been attained. These people who are now growing good crops of certain types are still unable to come in under the act. I received a couple of letters during this last spring with regard to people trying to get under the act; according to the department they are unable to do it because the land has been declared to be submarginal. I would ask the minister to look into some of those areas again. In view of improved methods and improved knowledge as to what crops should be grown, possibly some of these areas could now be included under the act because conditions have changed since they were taken out of the act or at least were left out of the act when the act was first incorporated into the law.

Mr. Chairman, the constituency of Yorkton happens to be one of those areas which have been greatly affected by flooding conditions during the last two or three years, and one particular area in the Assiniboine valley for even longer. The
Prairie Farm Assistance Act unusual water conditions of the past three years which have given parts of the prairie provinces an unusual rainfall and have caused the flooding out of much land which for years was productive farm land producing good crops makes an amendment to this act most necessary. I would say that, for the most part, the fact that flooded areas are being included under this act has been extremely welcome. Other parts of the amendment to the act under this bill will be criticized on good solid ground, in my opinion, when we come to them.
The people in the prairie provinces who went through the drought years are rather at a loss to understand why this change in weather conditions should so seriously affect them and they are wondering what the cause of it was. Ever since the flood in the Red river valley in 1950 the water table throughout Manitoba and now in eastern Saskatchewan has risen to such a point that much of the land is seriously affected, and last year there were signs that land would be going sour. I have seen good land-land which has never been known to have water on it before-flooded out and whole fields, because of the wet weather for a whole year, covered with a sort of green moss which forms on top of the soil and which is an indication of poor aeration and will lead ultimately to the souring of the land.
What was the cause of the Red river flooding I do not know. It just seemed to be that water seemed to be coming down into the Red river valley. The Red river rises in the United States. Whether there was an abnormal rainfall in that country I do not know. There may have been some diversion of water. I do not know what the facts are with regard to that matter. We do know the effect it has had upon the water tables of the two provinces. Manitoba is particularly hard hit.
The constituency of Yorkton in Saskatchewan has running through it, near Kamsack, a portion of the Assiniboine river valley. Because of the peculiar diagonal, the way in which the river runs through that part of the province, when the Assiniboine valley is flooded the floor of the valley becomes just like a lake; and because it runs in a diagonal way as much as 10,000 acres of arable land which has produced splendid crops-not only arable land but some of the best land-was river bottom. When there was not too much moisture this land produced some of the finest crops in the whole of the country. Just because of the diagonal way in which the river went through the constituency or through that township it was difficult if not utterly impossible to find a suitable block which would become eligible and which would qualify for payment under P.F.A.A.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act I can remember when the flooding occurred there in 1949. We made a request at that time that the federal government do something about flood control. I believe it is part of the ultimate plans of the Department of Agriculture under P.F.R.A. to place some dams on the upper portions of the Assiniboine valley and perhaps to do something about flood control in order to prevent that rush of water in the spring which leads to trouble in Saskatchewan and later on in Manitoba. If the minister can speed up that construction so that area can be controlled, I would urge him to do so. If the amendments will help in that matter, I am sure they will be welcomed by the people in that area.
Immediately north of Yorkton is the White-sand river. In the past two years there have been floods which have completely flooded out whole farms, some of them consisting of half a section. Some 80 per cent of the land which was previously cultivated has been completely flooded. This legislation is going to help them in a year or two. I notice in clause 1 which we are discussing at the present time the following:
(d) "cultivated land" means land that in the year of award was seeded to crop or was in summerfallow and includes . . .
(ii) land of a farmer that in three out of the five years immediately preceding the year of award had been seeded or summerfallowed, but owing to natural causes beyond his control could not be seeded or summerfallowed in the year of award;
This means that if an area became flooded for a period of say five years the land would no longer be eligible for payment under P.F.A.A. The actions of the government in building dams could easily affect the eligibility of a farmer from the point of view of whether or not his land could become eligible for award. I can see, and everyone will admit, that some restrictions are necessary. We certainly do not want to continue to pay awards for land that is going to be permanently flooded. I think something should be put in here to take care of such a situation, but the farmer certainly has no control over the flooding of his land and he is compelled to suffer very severe losses.
I find that some members are under the impression that a farmer who receives assistance under the act will be perfectly all right, but it should be understood that the maximum payments are naturally low. If a farmer has no crop at all and his land is eligible he is only covered to the extent of 200 acres. With no crop at all he would 

receive a maximum of $2.50 per acre, or a total of $500. If he has 4 bushels or less to the acre the limit is $300. Therefore I think the impression in the minds of some members of the house that this assistance really takes care of the farmer should be corrected. That might have been the case some years ago, but with the increasing costs of operation these payments do not begin to meet the farmer's costs. It merely means that he may be able to exist for another year and carry on with considerable debt in the hope that he will ultimately get a crop.
So far as the operation of the act this year is concerned, a good many farmers in eastern Saskatchewan have qualified because of rust damage to their crops. Many areas were marginal, and under the existing legislation the provision with respect to contiguous sections must have made administration quite difficult. In a general way I should like to make this suggestion to the minister if he wishes to improve the administration of the act. In the selection of inspectors I suggest that as far as possible he try not to pick somebody living too close to the particular area who may have relatives or friends in the region. I have received criticism to the effect that a brother, uncle, cousin or some relative of the inspector has appeared to receive preference and there seem to have been cases where other persons who were just as well qualified did not receive payments because they were not relatives or friends of the man in charge of the inspection staff.
It is a very difficult thing to administer properly, but I suggest to the minister that in the selection of inspectors he should make sure that kind of charge cannot be made.
I have not had a chance to investigate these cases personally and I am not making any charges, but these are some of the impressions I have received. May I say that so far as any correspondence I have had with his staff in Regina is concerned I have received prompt attention. When I have asked for reinspections the members of the staff have always said that they would consult the officials in the district. The service I have received as a member of the house has been very good, and some of the cases in which appeals have been made are still being investigated. I make this suggestion to the minister as something which will help to improve a very difficult situation and meet the pressing problems of people who are faced today with extremely high costs and

I should like to make a few
comments. Of course I do not know very much about the difficulties that the farmers of the west are having, but we are all interested because we will all have to pay whether we belong to the west or to the east. After listening to the members from the west, may I say that we realize the amendment is necessary, and I am sure there will be no objection. I do not know where people ever got the slogan, "Go west, young man, go west". Having seen the millions of dollars that have had to be paid out over a number of years under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, I am beginning to think that the people of our part of the country are pretty fortunate and that the slogan should now be changed to "Go east, young man", because we have no problems of this kind.
In all seriousness, I should like to ask the minister how many people in western Canada he estimates will be assisted and what will be the estimated cost of putting into force the provisions of the amendment. I think that is something that the people in other parts of Canada would be very anxious to know. As the previous speaker said, we realize that the maximum payment of $2.50 an acre for 200 acres is not going to make any farmer rich. It will be enough to meet a few of the necessities of life, but I think members of the house would be interested in knowing what the aggregate cost is going to be. Could the minister give us that information?

Mr. Chairman, in a sense I rise on a point of order, and I do so now because I did not want to interrupt the previous speaker. If we are to discuss the administration of the act I should like to have something to say about it, but I am rather of the opinion that administration of the act can be discussed on the minister's estimates and that that is the proper time rather than now.
That is the proper time to discuss it.
But if everyone is going to discuss administration now I want to participate in the discussion. I am quite willing to

In view of the questions that have been asked, I think I should probably say a few words. In common with the hon. member for Prince Albert, I expected that there would be a discussion on second reading and prepared my remarks accordingly. Therefore I find it a little difficult to stay entirely within the rules now in answering some of the questions that have been asked and some of the statements that have been made. However, I think I should do so, particularly in view of the suggestion just made by the hon. member from Nova Scotia-
New Brunswick.

I quite understand why you would not want to be associated with the gentleman behind you, but he is probably all right. Quite a few remarks have been made this morning which I think should be explained. I do not think any amendment of the nature of the one now before us would have been suggested at all except for the fact that practically all the people who will be affected by the legislation have paid into the fund far more than they will ever get out of it. This legislation will apply largely to the province of Manitoba and the northeastern section of Saskatchewan. Other areas are not very likely to come under it in any big way because there are not so many there who have suffered from extra water.
It may be that some places up in the northwestern and northeastern parts will receive some payments j but by far the greater amount of payments will be made in Manitoba and the northeastern part of Saskatchewan adjacent to Manitoba. That area has paid in very much more than it has taken out up until very recently. Manitoba, for example, paid in less the first year the act was in effect. That was the year of the great drought, as you will all recall, and Manitoba paid in $333,000 and drew out $905,000. Then in 1940 Manitoba paid in $354,000 and drew out $615,000. But, from there on, down to this year, Manitoba has never drawn out as much as they have paid in. The amounts they have received have been $36,000 in one year, $16,000 in another, $30,000 in another and $6,000 in another.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act They have been paying all the way along from $339,000 up to $1,331,000 and $1,400,000 in a year.
. But the most important part of that record is in the last four years. In the three years prior to 1954 Manitoba paid in $1,300,000, $1,400,000 and $973,000, and in the last year $385,000.
Would the minister put that whole table on the record?
I can put it on, if hon. members wish to have it.
We would find it helpful.

Then, in these last four years, in round figures, Manitoba drew out $207,000 as against $1,300,000; $185,000 as against $1,400,000, and in the next year they drew out $619,000 as against a payment of $973,000. The first year Manitoba has drawn out considerably more than they paid in was 1954-55. They paid in $385,000 and have drawn out $4,182,630. When you add that $4 million to the other three years, the fact is that they have drawn out for the four years the sum of $5,195,000 as against paying in $4,113,000.
I recite these figures only to indicate that the picture has changed. It has changed

to a considerable extent because of the fact that much of what is in the amendment, and therefore made clear to everyone that it is covered by the act, has been applied during this past year. As I said in the house before, we got an opinion from the Department of Justice as to whether we had authority to pay under the act, and they have said that we have. We went ahead and made payments. But anyone reading the act would perhaps find it difficult to find just where it was that we have that authority to pay under the act. So we are making it clear that authority is given to pay under certain circumstances.

The Saskatchewan position is such, of course, that there are far more people paying in Saskatchewan than anywhere else. As a matter of fact the farm population in that province is quite high. The exact figures, which I have before me, show a farm population in Manitoba of 52,383, and payments have been made to 23,440 or a little less than half. That is the number who have received payments this year. Then, the farm population of Saskatchewan is given as 112,000, in round figures, of whom 87,000 have received payments this year. In Alberta there are 84,000 farmers, of whom 32,000 have received payments this year.
The fact is that when one divides the $21,314,000 Saskatchewan farmers have received by the 87,000 farmers, it gives an amount of $245 per farmer.
Now, I would say this by way of comparison-and not by way of raising any criticism of anything else we may have done-that there were 2,000 apple growers in Nova Scotia who drew last year $967,000. Some of that will come back, of course, but the total amount paid out would be $483 per apple grower. That would have to be adjusted in order to take care of some amounts that were regained. But the payments made out in the first instance-*

And there is another point in connection with it that should be emphasized. We based our action in Nova Scotia on action that has been going on in Saskatchewan under this act from the very beginning. We pay the money to the farmer, and I think that was an important feature of the settlement made in Nova Scotia. We have not received a single


complaint, and I do not think even the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings who is perhaps more familiar with it than any other member in the house excepting the Minister of Public Works, and who has been familiar with the organization there for a long time, has had any complaints. The main feature that resulted in our having no complaints was that every dollar was put in the hands of the farmer, and that is true under this act. Every dollar paid out is paid to the farmer, and no one can make a claim against that man's money. It goes to the farmer, and he does what he likes with it.

No; I am speaking only
about what happened last summer as a result of the tornado which blew off 85 per cent of the apples. The government had nothing to do with the tornado.

The important point is that the payment is made to the farmer, not to a provincial government or to a municipality. We pay the money to the farmer, and he pays whatever bills he thinks he should pay.

speechtext: Are those farmers making any contributions to the fund, in the same way P.F.A.A. farmers are?

No, except through the fact they pay general taxes the same as others. They have not made a contribution. That is exactly the point I am making: this particular area that is to get the benefits of this amendment has paid in more. There is no one in any other part of Canada who is paying for these particular amendments. They are being paid for by the people who live in that area, because they have been paying in all through the period much more than they have drawn out, and now they are simply getting some of it back under the conditions that exist in that area.

Anything else he was able to buy after he got the money he bought it. Therefore, what is being paid into that area is $9,559,000. That is put into the pockets of the farmers and the farmer can pay his store bill. If he has enough money left to pay his taxes he pays his taxes. When he pays his taxes he makes it possible for the municipality to do road work. The fact that he has that amount of money helps him to assist his municipality and others to carry on.
Some suggestion has been made that the man who is in town and hires the work done on his farm should be paid under this act. The reason he is not paid under this act has just been outlined by me. This act was put on the statute books to make it possible for farmers who are farming land and who have gone through a period of crop failure to be on the land next year to produce a crop, the very thing mentioned by the hon. member for Selkirk. He says that the farmers are leaving the farms and going away because water is lying on their land. The objective of this legislation is to make it possible for these people to go to town and pay the food bill that they ran credit for last year, to pay for the clothing of their children that they ran credit for last year, so that they can go back to the store and get credit again this year. That is the objective of it. The amount of money that is provided for is not intended to be greater than the amount necessary for doing that kind of thing. Therefore we are simply suggesting here that that money ought to be in the hands-I think some of us would have said the same thing that was said with regard to family allowances if we had felt free to do so at the time-of the mother, but it is in the hands of the farmer, including the mother of course. That money is in -the hands of the people to do with as they see fit. This act provides for that kind of thing, and it is not intended to provide anything other than that. It is intended simply to make it possible for the farmer to stay there until the next year and produce another crop, so that section of the country can go on farming, as has been its custom.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a good deal of experience with this over the years, and I think we are to be complimented and the government is to be complimented on having an act of this kind. However, to make an act really effective in the minds of people, we must maintain confidence. I see that there is a lack of confidence here and there, not by reason of the general principle of prairie farm assistance, but from the standpoint that we have these blocks, and it does mean a certain unfairness in respect of payments. The unfairness is not intentional by any of the officials, I am sure. It is unfair by reason that we have these blocks of eligible or ineligible sections, with the result that a farmer who has a smaller yield than his neighbour may not get the payment while his neighbour living down the road or across the road has a high yield and gets the payment. By reason of that thing happening and of the fact that the act permits it to happen there is, of course, dissatisfaction.
Of course my plea is the same plea as that which we have been putting up from this corner of the house for a good many years. My plea is that the act should be adjusted in some fashion or other in order to make these payments on a sectional or unit basis. I know the minister has answered that question before. I should like to know why he has not changed his mind on this matter and why the government has not seen fit so to revise the act and to bring in amendments as to make this thing on a sectional or a unit basis.
There is unfairness, by reason of the fact that farmers who deserve payment because of low yield find that other farmers in the same area, or right next to them almost, have larger yields and get the payment. That situation is unfair and you cannot tell the farmer any different. There is the situation. It stares him in the face. You can explain the act. You can explain the reason for the block system. You can do all the explaining you like but you cannot explain away the fact that there is unfairness there.
This act is a sort of relief measure. The minister has said that. We have known it for a good many years. We knew it when the act was first brought in many years ago. The minister has rightly said that these payments are made in order to tide the farmer over so that he can pay his bills and stay on the farm until the next year. Let us compare this act with some other legislation that we have. Let us consider, for example, ordinary relief legislation that this government may assist the provinces with. You

Prairie Farm Assistance Act do not say to any community, "We are not going to pay this relief to the unfortunate people until a certain percentage of the working force of that community is unemployed". You do not do that. You calculate the thing on the individual basis.
Unemployment insurance is a similar thing in principle. Workers pay into the fund just in the same way as the farmers have paid into this fund. You do not say, "We will not pay this unemployment insurance until a block of workmen are out of work". You do not say that. As soon as the workman is out of work, if he is eligible under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act, he is paid. The principle of this act is the same as that in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not see why this act cannot be so adjusted as to bring it on the sectional or unit basis. Then the farmer would have confidence in it, knowing that when he got a low yield he would be sure of some measure of relief to tide him over.
I wish the minister would give some further explanation either as to the reason why he has not done so or as to whether he can offer any hope of any such changes.
