Order. Before the next order is called, perhaps I might be permitted to make a short statement. On June 14, during the debate on Bill No. 22, while I was in the chair a question of privilege was raised based on the assumption that an hon. member had discussed proceedings of a committee, meeting in camera. The question of privilege was to the effect that an hon. member, by discussing or divulging such proceedings, was committing a breach of the privileges of the house.
I said at the time that I did not feel competent to rule on the point at that time. Since then I have had an opportunity to consult authorities, living and written. I think the clearest explanation of the rights of members in this connection is to be found in May's fifteenth edition at page 610
"In Camera" Committee Proceedings where, after referring to the practice in the upper house, it is said:
Members of the House of Commons are likewise entitled to be present at the sittings of committees of their house, as well during the deliberations of the committee as while witnesses are being examined; and though, if requested to retire, they rarely make any objection, and ought, on the grounds of established usage and courtesy to the committee, immediately to retire when the committee is about to deliberate, the committee, in case of their refusal, has no power to order them to withdraw. As members cannot be excluded from a committee room by the authority of the committee, the committee, if it desires that other members should not be present at its proceedings, and such members refuse to withdraw, should adjourn and, if they persist in attending at subsequent meetings, the committee should apply to the house for power to effect their exclusion.
Later on the same work says:
When, in the opinion of either house, secrecy ought to be maintained, secret committees, or, as they are termed in the commons, committees of secrecy are appointed, whose proceedings and inquiries are conducted throughout with closed doors; and it is the invariable practice for all members, not being of the committee, to be excluded from the committee room throughout the whole of its proceedings.
Similar pronouncements are to be found in Beauchesne's third edition, citations 552 and 551, and Bourinot at pages 468 and 469, also in May's thirteenth edition at pages 476 and 477.
From these it is obvious that there is a distinct difference between committees sitting in camera for the purposes of deliberation, and secret committees. These remarks apply only to committees meeting in camera.
It is established by the authorities that all members of the Commons have a legal right to attend such meetings, but not to participate in their deliberations. The proceedings of the meetings then are, if I may put it this way, the property of the House of Commons, of course only after the committee has reported. So no true question of privilege arises if a member divulges to the house the proceedings of such meetings.
However, it should also be stated immediately that the purpose behind in camera meetings is that the members may feel free to negotiate, to discuss, to deliberate and sometimes perhaps to compromise without the glare of publicity which might add to the difficulties of agreeing to reports, etc.; and it would seem to be desirable that these proceedings should be treated as in confidence. But the final decision rests with the members themselves. Technically the privileges of the house are not involved.

the

On a point of order, I was not able to hear. Would you tell us which bill is now before the house?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: BiU No. 427, letter L-14 of the Senate, an act for the relief of Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme.

In that case I think I ought to read the bill that is actually before us. I know it is not customary to supply members of parliament with copies of the bills, except
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
that a copy of the bill appears as one of the first few pages of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special committee of the other place. This bill reads as follows:
An act for the relief of Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme.
Whereas Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme, domiciled in Canada and residing at the town of Pointe-aux-Trembles, in the province of Quebec, car salesman, has by his petition alleged that on the thirteenth day of August, A.D. 1931, at the said town, he and Antoinette Seguin, who was then of the said town, a spinster, were married; and whereas by his petition he has prayed that, because of her adultery since then, their marriage be dissolved; and whereas the said marriage and adultery have been proved by evidence adduced and it is expedient that the prayer of his petition be granted:	Therefore Her Majesty,
by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows;
1.	The said marriage between Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme and Antoinette Seguin, his wife, is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever.
2.	The said Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme may at any time hereafter marry any woman whom he might lawfully marry if the said marriage with the said Antoinette Seguin had not been solemnized.
This is a draft bill approved by the committee on divorce of the Senate in May, 1955. The bill is signed by A. W. Roebuck, chairman of the committee on divorce.
I put this on the record so the country will know exactly what has happened. In discussing the principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker, a little consideration should be given to exactly who is this man, Joseph Delphis Guillaume Delorme, the petitioner in this case, who appears before both houses of parliament of Canada and asks that he be given relief from his marriage vows. A year ago he was listed as a taxi driver. This year he is listed as a car salesman.
I should like to indicate to the house the type of people who impose these burdens on the parliament of Canada, and especially so in this case. I cannot be more effective than by reading my poor translation of an article that appeared in Id, Montreal, of June 5 of last year. On page 7 it says:
William Delorme appeared, the 21st of April last, on a charge of the attempted rape of one Mary Staiguill; he must attend a preliminary hearing and will remain meanwhile at liberty on bail of $950 which his father has furnished, giving as security for the presence of the accused, his property, valued at $10,000.
The reason I read that into the record, Mr. Speaker, was to give an indication to the country at large of the type of individual who is by this method permitted to occupy the time of the two houses of Canada's parliament.
Was he convicted?

In fairness to Mr. Delorme I must say that the charge against him was later reduced to one of assault. I do not know what happened. However, the very fact that the man was arrested on a charge of that sort is an illustration to prove the validity of the remark I made that very many of these people are completely unworthy of the time of both houses of Canada's parliament.
Let us look for a minute at the argument that this hero makes in asking us for relief from his marriage vows. He uses the argument in the evidence that on numerous occasions since the year 1938 he has personally witnessed his wife committing acts of adultery. In order to further show the type of individuals who have the audacity to impose on Canada's houses of parliament I should read a little bit of the record just to indicate the type of individual we are dealing with here. He says that in 1938 he first became aware of the adulterous nature of his wife. He admits that on page 16 of the evidence, and then the following questions and answers appear:
Q. And what happened when you came into the house?
A. I saw them in bed.
Q. And then what?
A. I went away.
Q. Where did you go in the house?
A. I went in the door, went in the room and saw the two of them together, and 1 went away crying.
Q. What?
A. I went away crying.
Q. Did you wake them up?
A. No, I did not.
Q. You did not even wake them up?
A. No, I did not.
Q. And on the second time or occasion you say it was in the afternoon. Where were they that afternoon?
A. In the same place.
Q. Where, in the house?
A. This was in my mother's bedroom, that is another room.
Q. What were they doing?
A. Sleeping, and they were in bed and he was on top.
Q. Did you wake them up or were they asleep?
A. I just went home again crying.
I am going to skip a little bit. He speaks of another occasion.

On a point of order, I suggest that this evidence has been given before special committees, and this is not the proper place for details of these cases to be read. It is usual to refer bills of this kind to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, and that is why I moved second reading. I expected that it would go there and the details could then be discussed in the miscellaneous private bills committee and the bill be reported once again to this house.
Private Bills-Divorce

If I may speak on the point
of order which has been raised, I do not believe it is unheard of in this house to use evidence which has been produced before a committee of either of the houses of parliament in order to illustrate a certain basic principle. I was attempting to show the type of individual this Mr. Delorme is. There were two cases in 1938 where he found his wife in the act of committing adultery, and in neither case did he even take the trouble nor was he man enough to as much as attempt to deal with the other man. He quietly sneaked away. According to his testimony, on the third occasion he found this act being committed in his own home and once again, according to his evidence, he got his hockey pass and simply went to the hockey game, crying again. Then he was asked if it was not rather odd that he should have acted like that, and his reply was that he loved his family so much that he did nothing about it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before you rule on the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that at five o'clock a ruling was given by the deputy chairman of committees, who was occupying Your Honour's place in the house at the time, with regard to revealing what went on in a committee that had met in camera. I listened with considerable interest to the ruling, which was to the effect that there is no violation of privilege through using such information. The hon. gentleman who was then occupying the chair said it would be up to each individual member to decide what he should do. In view of that ruling the point of order raised by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Fairey) is hardly valid.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am perfectly aware of the ruling which was given at five o'clock with respect to a question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) on the bill relating to box cars, in connection with which an amendment had been moved by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). Matters which had occurred in a standing committee while studying its report were discussed and a distinction was drawn between a committee meeting in secrecy and one which was meeting in camera.
At the moment we are not dealing with a committee which was meeting in camera. The Senate committee on divorce meets, the evidence is printed and distributed to members of both houses. The hon. member could not quote from the evidence if it had not been reported and printed. The hon. member is doing what has been done quite often in this house, quoting from the evidence in

Private Bills-Divorce
discussing the second reading of a bill. I agree with the hon. member tor Victoria, B.C. to a certain extent, that when we discuss the second reading of a private bill we are not deciding by our vote the principle of that bill, we are merely passing the bill conditionally upon proper evidence being presented in the standing committee to support it. That is why the rules refer all private bills to standing committees.
This is a point which has interested me considerably over the years. Why should hon. members of the House of Commons, when discussing the second reading of a private bill which has come from the Senate where it has been studied by a committee, review the evidence which has been presented before that committee? If an hon. member wants to make representations, why not let the bill pass conditionally to the standing committee, at which time witnesses could be called for cross-examination? There is no remedy in what an hon. member may say here on the second reading of a bill.
I make these remarks, not for the purpose of ruling out what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is doing at the moment, but simply to remind hon. members that although they have a right to refer to evidence presented before the committee on divorce of the Senate, I would think a more effective course to adopt would be to have such evidence reviewed by the standing committee to which the bill would be referred.
I offer this opinion merely by way of suggesting that this course should be followed in order to expedite business in the house. But the hon. member is perfectly in order in reading the evidence in the way he has been doing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Would Your Honour permit a comment on what you have just said? I want to say that I agree thoroughly with your contention that there is a difference between the second reading of a public bill and the second reading of a private bill. No doubt Four Honour's opinion is based upon citation 769 of Beauchesne's third edition. However, 1 feel that there are one or two sentences of that citation which should be placed on the record. The citation says in part:
A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.

That is exactly what Your Honour said in your own perhaps better chosen words, but let me go on and quote the citation further:
Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee. This is the first occasion on which the bill is before the house otherwise than pro forma or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
I understand that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam believes that the principle of this bill is objectionable, and he is attempting its defeat on second reading. He does not think it should even go to the committee for examination. I suggest that while what Your Honour said in general regarding private bills is perfectly correct, there is the qualification that if a bill is felt to be particularly objectionable an hon. member would be within the four corners of citation 769 in attempting its defeat at this stage.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has drawn our attention to citation 769 which states:
Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable-
In stating his opinion that the principle is objectionable the hon. member would be discussing facts which have been submitted to the committee of the other place. I submit that the best way for the hon. member to dispute those facts or to comment upon them would be to have witnesses called before our committee for cross-examination.
That does not detract from the position I have taken. As I say, if the hon. member wishes to carry on, it has been the practice in the past that evidence has been reviewed on the second reading of these bills; but as far as my personal opinion is concerned- and perhaps I should not volunteer it at this stage-that is not as effective a method of opposing the principle of a bill. It may be that, unless I was prepared to make a ruling based on these views, this would be better left unsaid, but I am interested in expediting the business of the house and that is the only reason I mention them.

I wonder if I may be granted the privilege of explaining why I raised the point of order. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would allow me, I would like to say that this particular case is an objectionable one and I share the hon. member's concern over it.

speechtext: The hon. member for Victoria, B.C., asked the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam if he would give way. This case was before the Senate committee in 1954, and it was recommended to this house and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills. It was brought back into this house and discussion arose and, as hon. members will remember, it died on the order paper. The petitioner then applied once again for divorce to the Senate committee. The case was reheard.
No.

Excuse me. I have the evidence here. The case was reheard in this manner, that at the first meeting of the Senate committee on divorce a discussion arose as to whether the evidence presented to last year's committee was admissible, and it was agreed that it would be. Subsequently the petitioner, the lady, through her lawyer, wrote to say she had decided not to continue the case on second hearing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: She was the respondent.
I beg your pardon. I shall correct that. The respondent, through her solicitor, wrote to say she would not defend the case.
She did not have the money.

Let us not examine the reasons. I am stating the fact that the solicitor wrote to say that she would not defend the case. I am not stating the reasons for it, as I do not wish to take the time of the house to do so. At a subsequent meeting on May 6 of this year, the case was resumed before the
Private Bills-Divorce
Senate committee, and the respondent appeared with three additional witnesses. Those witnesses were heard. The case was reviewed and reported to the main committee of the Senate, and they still recommended the divorce. That is the bill before us now.
I may say something that I omitted, Mr. Speaker. Last year when the bill was first referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills of this house, we ourselves actually heard the evidence once again, with witnesses and legal representatives present. At that time our own committee on miscellaneous private bills recommended the bill on division, and it was talked out in the house and died on the order paper.
What we have, then, is a divorce bill which is, I admit, an objectionable one and, as I said before, I also have concern about it. It was recommended last year, it was tried before the Senate committee, it was tried before our own committee, it was still recommended to this house, it has been tried again by the Senate committee, and now comes before us again.
The reason I raised the point of order and why I am speaking now is that I think the proper procedure is that this house should be spared the gruesome details, and that we should pass this bill on second reading and refer it to the committee on miscellaneous private bills for whatever action that committee cares to take on it. I do not think this house needs to know all the nasty details, with which this evidence is replete.

Mr. Speaker, may I assure both yourself and the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., that it certainly is far from my intention to put on record the gruesome details of this case. What I did put on the record was not put there in order to convict either the petitioner or the respondent. I thought I had made it perfectly clear that I found it necessary to put certain things on the record in order to show to the people of Canada the type of individual to which this parliament and the other house of parliament is willing to devote so much time.
I am quite prepared to leave the individual's record as I gave it, except that I must add that I read from the record that the man had known of this adultery since 1938, and he admits having lived with the woman until some time in 1952. It was only after the wife sued him for a separation order in the province of Quebec and was awarded $20 a week, plus a division of the community property, that the man's shoe really started to hurt. He then decided he had better rid himself of his wife by the misuse of the

Private Bills-Divorce
houses of parliament of Canada and thus relieve himself of these two financial obligations which were rightfully imposed upon him by a court in the province of Quebec.
He appeared to put forth his plea, and what did he use to substantiate it? This raises a basic principle as well. Exactly what are acceptable witnesses in these cases? I found it very hard, after listening all day a year ago, to decide who was being honest and who was being dishonest in the case, and I think most members of the committee had very much the same feeling. However, what is an acceptable witness? One of the main witnesses in the case is a man by the name of Nadeau. I have a letter here from a young air force man written to my colleague the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), dated June 15, in which he has this to say-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member at this point merely to ask him if he thinks that, in discussing the principle of a divorce bill, he is entitled to question the responsibility or morality or other qualifications of a witness who appeared before a committee in the other place. I would ask him to ponder this question very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, on that point, the very basis on which we are asked to agree is that evidence is supposed to have been presented in these cases that adultery has been
committed,	and this evidence has been accepted by a committee of the other house. In most cases a special committee of three examines it and later reports to a larger
committee.	I raised this point a year ago, on this point of order, and asked the Minister of Justice what follow-through there might possibly be. He finally came forward with an answer, and as a result of my asking the question I think two men were found guilty of having committed perjury. They won their appeal on a technicality.
But, Mr. Speaker, when we are asked to pass on the principle of a case, on second reading, and when we find what happened in some cases, as in the case of one particular hero investigator last year, who handled no less than 88 cases before the other house, I feel that we are perfectly within our rights in calling before this parliament and the bar of public opinion the authenticity of what is happening in these cases.
The other case which yesterday you saw fit to rule out of order-and I am not going to argue that-was that of a man who testified in 75 other cases, and there were three separate instances where he had a double win on the one evening. That's an almost impossible situation, and one which is made the more unbelievable when you realize that within

five days of one divorce the man got married to the woman who won her divorce.
Again, I did not intend to introduce the bill referred to yesterday and I shall attempt not to refer to it again. I intended to introduce a bill on another case that I think would have made this Delorme case look rather ridiculous. Unfortunately the woman, who was willing to testify before a committee of parliament that she herself had committed perjury in order to obtain her divorce, passed away only a few months ago.
This racket must be cleaned up in one way or the other, and the only way we have of doing it is by using this floor of parliament to call the attention of the general public of Canada to the racket that is going on and the needless misery being inflicted upon thousands of women who are unable to defend themselves in the proper manner, and who allow themselves finally to be intimidated and in most cases appeal to this parliament and profess to sue their husbands for divorce.
What happened in this particular case? Last year we see that this case was heard by hon. Senators Bradley, Golding and Kinley. This year, as the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., says, they met again on May 6 and the case was reheard by hon. Senators Roebuck, Golding and Barbour. It will be noted that two of the three were not the same as those who acted a year ago. Then there was a consideration of the proceedings on May 9 by hon. Senators Bradley, Golding and Kinley. It was then referred and recommended by them to the committee of the whole, and eventually it passed the other place.
Speaking on the principle of this thing, on January 12 or 13 in the throne speech debate I appealed to the Prime Minister to find a way by which parliament might be relieved of this onerous responsibility.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is making a general case with respect to the procedure which should be followed in matters of divorce. All we are dealing with now is a bill allowing two persons to be divorced. That is all that is before us at the moment. When the hon. member begins to generalize as to the quality of witnesses and the method of proceeding with divorce bills, I think he is getting away from the principle of this bill. I do not recall whether or not the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre introduced his bill this session to make the exchequer court a court where divorce cases could be heard, but 1 know he did so in past sessions. The bill he introduced is precisely the type of bill on which could be raised these questions

which the hon. member now wants to raise, but they cannot be raised on a specific divorce bill.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In coming back to this specific bill that is before us may I say that we are asked to endorse the principle on second reading and to refer this bill to the committee of this house. My contention is that no such thing should happen. This bill is unworthy of consideration by the committee of this house.
We make a decision in this house. That decision will either keep Mr. and Mrs. Delorme married to one another or it will grant the relief for which Mr. Delorme is petitioning. I have often heard it said that we ought to take the attitude that this Delorme marriage is broken up anyway, and therefore we might as well let the bill slide through. To me that is no argument, Mr. Speaker. I have never met nor heard of a judge in any law court who rendered a decision without giving careful consideration to the effect of his decision. I think that is a basic truth in British justice. I think it also applies here.
If we divorce these people-just as when we agree to the divorce of any other two people-we are saying in effect that we have found one or the other guilty of having committed adultery. In some parts of Canada that finding may perhaps be lived down, but there are other sections of Canada where this finding brands these people for the rest of their lives, and it brands their offspring as well. One of their parents has been found by the parliament of Canada to have committed adultery. That is the effect of what we do when we pass one of these acts. It is hardly good enough for us to say, "Oh, it is up to the provincial law; we have nothing to do with that". We must give consideration to the effect of our legislation here, whether the legislation has to do with a pipe-line company or whether it deals with the dissolution of the Delorme marriage contract.
What happened last year? The case was dealt with by a vote of this house. I should like to thank hon. members from the province of Quebec for helping us in getting this bill referred to the committee of this house on third reading. I think they were loyal to their convictions, and they showed it by getting up in their places and voting as they did. Also by their actions in the committee they remained loyal to their convictions.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to move an amendment to this clause. Before doing so, however, I should like to say a few words in connection with the subject matter. I have examined the minutes of proceedings of the standing committee on privileges and elections that studied this bill, and I find there was no prolonged debate in that committee.
This change was made on the recommendation of the chief electoral officer. However, he did not express very strong views in the matter. After having set forth the possible consequences of errors in the lists of candidates sent to the armed forces outside of Canada, when the delay was one of 14 days, the chief electoral officer said this did not happen at the last election. At that time we had troops in Korea, but it is not likely that we will have them there at the time of the next election. Let me add that a law should not be passed to cover exceptions; it should be of general application.
The chief electoral officer expressed the administrative point of view. However, there are other points of view, such as that of the public interest. As expressed in Mr. Castonguay's evidence, the chief objection raised in the past to the extension of the period between nomination day and polling day is that it would reduce the time for political groups in the country to choose their candidates. I submit, Mr. Chairman, it is definitely in the public interest that plenty of time be given for the choice of candidates so the high standard of representation which exists in this house may be maintained in the future. It is quite clear that quite a number of hon. members feel that this period of 14 days should not be increased, and it will be admitted that each member of the house should be elected under conditions acceptable to all.
If the status quo is maintained I believe it will not prejudice anyone in the house. In making these remarks I do not in any manner blame the chief electoral officer for the suggestion he has made. As indicated, he presented the administrative point of view, but he did not press the point. Therefore I move:

speechtext:
I am very pleased that the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska has introduced this amendment, and the minister has indicated that he does not disapprove of or oppose it. I would point out that this has stood for many years, and that there have been good reasons for the 14-day period. All hon. members here realize that there is an advantage in ample preliminary time being available to consider the question of candidates and other details of that kind. I would point out that we have a rather long election period here. We read with interest recently that in the United Kingdom, where their elections are considered very important, the whole election campaign took less than a month.
I do not think it is an advantage to unduly increase the period of the campaign, and the procedure adopted in this case would have that effect. The only reason that was actually given for the increase was the problem that might be raised in connection with the vote of any armed forces overseas. Every hon. member here would be prepared to agree that anything that was desirable from the point of view of making it possible for members of the armed forces to exercise their democratic right should be considered favourably. After all, if there are any people who have the right to a democratic process in a satisfactory way it is those who themselves are taking the first responsibility for democracy.
My own submission is that it is not a real problem at all. If there has been any confusion in the lists it is not because of the difference between the 14-day period and the 21-day period. We must remember that the moment an election is announced and in fact well before that-because the government usually does not decide at the last moment- appropriate steps are taken to ensure that returning officers will be in position in adequate time.
In so far as the printing of the lists is concerned, that is something that can easily be done within the 14-day period. After all, with cables to any main centres, with wireless to any military centres, it is possible actually within minutes of the close of nominations to flash to any part of the world the complete list of the nominated candidates. All military units have printing devices available to

them by which the appropriate lists can be prepared. Therefore, with the advantages of cable and wireless and the available printing services, so long as the details are arranged the 14-day period is ample. It has stood there for a long time and for adequate reasons.
I have mentioned the situation in regard to the armed forces because, as some hon. members know, I have had occasion to assume some responsibility in regard to that matter myself on earlier occasions. I know it can be done satisfactorily within the 14-day period so long as the preliminary details are arranged. I would hope, therefore, that the amendment proposed will be supported by everyone on both sides of the house.

The section of the act reads: -the said judge shall appoint a time within four days after receipt of the said affidavit to recount the said votes.
As the hon. member has said, that section was found to be susceptible of another interpretation. A judge might fix a date within four days, but then the date fixed for the recount might be two or three months after the four days have elapsed. The clause of the bill reads:
-such judge shall appoint a time to recount the said votes, which time shall, subject to subsection (3), be within four days after the receipt of the said affidavit.
I would not think that is susceptible to the other interpretation. I believe the clause as it now reads makes it mandatory that the date be fixed and the recount take place within that time.
Mr.1 Casileden: The hon. member for Selkirk was the one involved. The hon. member applied for a recount because the vote was fairly close. The judge set September 28 as the date. When September 28 came along nothing had happened, and my hon. friend who had applied for the recount wondered what was being done. On inquiry he was told that the judge was not feeling very well, that he had had a heart attack or something and was no longer on the bench. Another judge was appointed to take his place, which I presume would be done by the Department of Justice. This other judge then took it upon himself to declare that the decision of the first judge with regard to the recount was wrong. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for the benefit of those who are getting worried because the wheels are spinning too rapidly, we are simply passing a number of forms authorized in the act. Clause 35 deals with the voting of service personnel. I should like to draw the attention of the minister particularly to this definition of the outer envelope in which the service personnel vote is deposited after the voter has marked his ballot. I know it is a matter of administration, and I do not know whether it is possible to deal with it in the

Canada Elections Act act, but I want to impress it upon the minister. I know he, in consultation with the electoral officer, will try to deal with the situation.
I myself am satisfied that the machinery which is provided by this act for the voting of service personnel, if properly carried out, retains absolute secrecy of the ballot of the particular service personnel voter. Nevertheless the machinery is such that they write out the vote in their own handwriting and put it in a small white envelope, and this in turn they put in a so-called outer envelope, which we are dealing with now. On the outside of the outer envelope they have to write their name and declare that they are John Brown, who is entitled to vote.
I am sure that 75 per cent of them believe that in that way their ballot can be identified. In other words they do not believe that electoral officers can be so scrupulously correct that they can open the outer envelope, as I believe they do, and draw out the white envelope and drop it in the box without looking at it. I have talked to scores of service personnel, and every one of them says, "Of course, they see my name on the envelope and they know how I vote". It has quite an effect.
I hope when this machinery is carried into effect the chief electoral officer and the officers of the armed forces will give all possible publicity to this, and give guarantees of the fact that when the outer envelope is opened, the inner envelope is taken out and put into the box. Once it goes in the box it loses the connecting link with the outer envelope, and there can be no identification. I believe that is the subject of a great deal of comment among service personnel, and I think in some way that doubt should be cleared up in their minds.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext: There is a good deal in what the hon. member has said. There may be the thought in the mind of the member of the service that the putting of his name on the envelope will identify him as the one who voted for a given candidate, although the ballot itself is contained in another envelope. I do not see any other way than to draw this to their attention and inform all members of the services that the purpose of the inner envelope is precisely to avoid that situation. I do not see very much in the way of another solution to the problem, but I shall draw this matter to the attention of the electoral officer.

I think some machinery could be worked out. We developed one method, that of putting it in the big brown envelope, and we are getting this result.

What we are doing here is to provide the franchise for the wives of service personnel who are serving abroad. As I read these regulations, the wife will be compelled to vote for the candidate in the polling area or polling district for which her husband originally registered, although I think there is a good chance that she may never have lived in that area herself.

On the whole, the committee considered that it was better to give the vote to the wives even though some possible difficulties in administration were created, rather than deprive them of the vote. It is an experiment. The chief electoral officer prepared regulations which I think can be made to work. It is a most interesting experiment and one which I think the whole house and the country generally will be interested in following.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if I might suggest the procedure. I think it would probably be desirable if the committee considered first the resolutions to which I referred in the budget speech, and then came back to those to which I referred on June 2.

That seems to be a convenient arrangement.
I want to make one or two preliminary remarks which also partly refer to procedure. But before I even do that, I want to refer to two items of interest. They are of interest particularly in connection with tariff matters, and they appeared in the morning press. One is an editorial in the Globe and Mail which refers to legislation in the United States which is of great interest to us. I shall read briefly from it:
Both houses of congress at Washington have now passed the bill which the Eisenhower administration considers the most important item on its 1955 agenda, the three-year extension of the reciprocal trade agreements act. Under this measure, he-
That is, the President.
-will be able to reduce tariffs by 15 per cent during the next three years and to cut any tariff levy above 50 per cent down to that level. The concessions permitted by this twenty-one-year-old law may be made by the President in return for similar concessions agreed to by any other nation, without reference to either congress or the tariff commission.
Customs Tariff
The second item I wish to read from briefly refers to the annoying but sometimes serious techniques of the administration of tariff laws. I read from a Canadian Press dispatch appearing in the Globe and Mail of today as follows:
Every year Canadian and United States businessmen pay out thousands of dollars to fight long, drawn-out disputes arising from an invisible curtain of tariffs.
These are the so-called "peek-a-boo" tariffs, the procedural red tape, the niceties of tariff language that are not immediately apparent to the shipper until he moves goods into a market and suddenly finds he has to pay extra tariff charges.
That whole item is worth reading, but I do not propose to take up the time of the committee in order to read it all. I think it is of interest to mention it because it refers to matters which are of such great importance in connection with our tariff relations, and we know how important they are.
I wish to make a couple of suggestions with regard to procedure. In his speech on April 5 the minister spoke in general about the tariff changes. Reading from page 2738 of Hansard of April 5, the minister said:
Many of them are essentially formal, but they serve to bring the wording of individual tariff items into line with changing trade practices and changing technology. Others make permanent certain temporary reductions in our tariffs on materials imported for use in Canadian manufacturing, reductions that were originally introduced by order in council in past years on a trial basis. Still others provide for new tariff reductions.
I suggest that the minister should make a brief comment on that. I should like to know a little about the order in council practice, the power for reductions made by order in council and just how they are followed through, partly in timing and partly in other ways, in the house. The minister then went on to say that the change in revenues will not be significant. He speaks about Canadians returning from abroad, and what he says there seems to be satisfactory. Then he goes on to speak about certain tariff changes in detail, and I suggest-indeed, I hope-the minister will go through the items explaining generally the reason for their being there.
For instance, there are two pages of items at the outset dealing with sugar, and so far as my observation goes there is no change in tariff. The minister will presumably explain that. Then there is the same thing with respect to aeroplane parts, and in many cases I observe there are no changes in tariffs. I suggest that the minister should go down the list and make general comments with regard to those where there is no change in tariff rates, but should comment specifically on those where there are changes in

Customs Tariff
tariff rates. That is going to take a little time, but it seems to me that is the common-sense way to deal with it.
Then there are one or two comments I want to make. Some of the changes result from reports of the tariff board, and the minister will no doubt refer to them. Then at page 2739 the minister goes on to say that he is going to refer two other sections to the tariff board, one having to do with the chemical industry and another having to do with the primary iron and steel schedule. Speaking on the latter, he says that it was worked out many years ago and badly needs overhauling. I should like the minister to comment on that, because on its face it seems as if we are a little late on the job. I wish the minister would comment on that at whatever length is necessary to make the situation clear. I suggest that is a reasonable way to proceed with the matter. It involves a certain amount of detail, but on the other hand it seems to me we cannot do less than ask to have the actual tariff changes explained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I shall answer part of what my hon. friend has asked. My parliamentary assistant is going to deal with the items that are under discussion. However, there are two general questions to which the hon. member referred. The first has to do with the reduction of tariffs by order in council. This is provided for in section 273 of the Customs Act, subsection (j) and (1), I think it is, which gives the governor in council the power to reduce tariffs upon recommendation of the Minister of Finance. I have discovered that there are a considerable number of these requiring signature from time to time. The principles, of course, are many and varied. The main purpose is to see that materials are admitted to Canada as cheaply as possible when they will be of use in Canadian manufacturing.
Did the minister say section 273 of the Customs Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. With respect to the other question as to the reference to the tariff board of the primary iron and steel schedule, I am afraid I cannot amplify very much what I said on the night of the budget address. My recollection is that these items have not been changed to any appreciable extent since 1937, and in the meantime our industry has grown by leaps and bounds. Some of the items do not bear any relation to present production methods, any more than the chemical items have reference to what is now being produced. For example, so far as the chemical items are concerned I am told

that there are far more items not being produced now that are covered by tariff than items now being produced that are covered.
In other words, customs and trade practices change, and you have new products almost yearly, if not monthly. For that reason tariff items which at one time covered something in general use no longer cover items in general use, and in the meantime other items have come into general use. The question is whether they ought to be covered by new items in the customs tariff. I submit that my words were properly used when I said the items were worked out many years ago and badly need overhauling. There has not been a general study of these particular items since before the second world war, and it seems to me wise that the tariff board should be entrusted with that duty at the present time.
You will also notice, Mr. Chairman, that we have referred other items to the tariff board, and others will be referred from time to time, but in keeping with the practice since the tariff board was first established we will not undertake any major changes in tariff items without a thorough study by the board before we recommend it to parliament.

My question really did not involve surprise that it was desirable to overhaul the tariff items. The minister's words have now underlined the fact that it is 18 years since the primary iron and steel schedule was covered, and I suggest we may probably have more to say about that when the bill is before us. We need not pursue it at the moment, but I suggest the minister might look into that with a view to discussing the matter further, because 18 years does seem a long time.

This has to do with the imposition of duties to offset a subsidy. Supposing you have the case such as I understand does exist, of a tax on goods being exported; does that offset the subsidy, or affect the position?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I had some difficulty in following what the hon. member was saying.

This resolution provides that where there is a subsidy in a country of export, a tariff may be put on to equal that amount. Supposing, as I understand does exist-and it seems odd from our point of view-that there is a country where there is a local tax on goods being exported, what happens then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It depends upon what we consider the purpose of the tax to be. If there is a domestic reason for the tax, not obviously connected with subsidizing rather than stimulating exports, then we would not consider it as something about which action should be taken under this proposed legislation. This is generally confined to those cases where there has been a state subsidy, which results in a price for export which under the circumstances is not considered fair.

Then you concern yourself wholly with the price at which the exporter is able to export; is that correct? If he has a subsidy which enables him to bring his price down, then that enures to his benefit, but you retain the right to impose a tariff to offset that. I am not clear as to what happens if there is an export tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend has read the resolution and my explanation on June 2. I think we would have to look at the tax to see its effect on our trade. I cannot imagine an export tax as such which would lower the price with respect to importation, although there may be one. However, if my hon. friend has any point in mind I would like to discuss it with him.
I shall leave it until we come to the bill.
May I ask whether any particular cases were in mind which gave rise to this proposal? Are there any examples the minister could cite of subsidized goods which would be affected by this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not know what the fault is, but I have not been able to hear hon. members opposite. I do not know whether our amplifying system is working. I understand the question was whether I had any particular items in mind. The difficulty in stating any given item at the moment is obvious. There will be tariff changes made by order in council passed pursuant to this
[Mr. Harris.!
legislation. As is customary, one does not give notice of that before the event.

I take it we can rely on the fact that no specific order in council is drawn and ready to be put into force. I think the minister should give that undertaking now. If any action is taken under this section, it will be taken after an interval so there will be opportunity to make representations before the order in council is dealt with?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On these orders, and for the reason I have already given, no immediate action is expected; but it does provide in our legislation for the kind of action which apparently may have to be taken, and provides legislation which I am told is in effect in many other countries and which we have not had so far in Canada.

That is all right so far as it goes. The minister will see my point. What I am concerned about is that if this power is given and orders in council are passed under this section, then presumably it could be done without those concerned knowing about it and no opportunity may be given for protest. A good deal will depend upon the practice which is followed in using this power, so those who might be affected by it can be heard and their cases considered before the orders in council are put into effect.

The resolution refers to subsidies direct or indirect. So far as goods directly subsidized by a government outside of Canada are concerned, we shall probably find that out without too much difficulty. When we come to an interpretation of indirectly subsidized goods we are taking in an awful lot of territory.
Let me give an example. In the United States or some other country that exports to Canada they are producing something on irrigated land, on which irrigation works are built and supported by the government. There would be an indirect subsidy, to the extent that the government spends money to irrigate this land or provides the equipment, or makes a grant toward that work to grow this produce. In an instance of that kind, would the minister say that was an indirectly subsidized product?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I would -not expect that would be considered an indirect subsidy for the purpose of this legislation. Direct and indirect in this connection means a subsidy affecting export. In my opinion it would not be an article which somewhere along the way in the normal course of domestic policy might have some form of subsidy.

It does not say so in the resolution. The resolution reads:
Where in the opinion of the governor in council subsidized goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada are or may be directly or indirectly imported into Canada he may declare such goods to be subject to an additional duty on their importation equal to the amount of the subsidy on those goods as determined by him.
There is nothing in the resolution to say that this refers to goods which are for export only. It refers to goods which are directly or indirectly subsidized which may or may not be exported. Of course, that takes in every article that is made, because everything is potentially exportable, and no one can say that a particular type of goods is exportable and another is not. I think that takes in the whole field, particularly when you get down to 2 (a) (i), which states:
A subsidy has been paid directly or indirectly by a government outside Canada, or any agency thereof.
That takes in a very wide field. I should like to have explained to us the purpose of this resolution. Second, what is considered to be an indirect subsidy as distinct from a direct subsidy, and wherein does it restrict the powers with respect to goods which are for export only? At the present time it takes in the whole field; it makes it possible for the government, by order in council, to declare an extra duty on any article they may desire. There is no restriction; there is no specification; it is a blanket policy, so far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I gave one concrete example of what was intended to be covered by this resolution, where a particular country, having acquired a lot of goods by purchase, sought to export them to Canada at a lower price than it paid. It may have been an unconscious subsidy in the sense that when they purchased the goods in the first instance they may not have intended to export them. In fact I do not think they did. Nevertheless, having those goods on hand they felt they should dispose of them in this manner, and there was a direct or indirect subsidy, if you like, to the extent of the difference between their cost and the intended sale price.
That was the one example I felt I could give and should give; but there are, as my hon. friend knows quite well, a number of countries in the world that are now seeking to export goods using every device they can think of to make the price attractive, which is in the form of a subsidy. This legislation is for the purpose of protecting commodities that are produced in this country against that type of subsidized importation into Canada.

I should like to ask this question. Is this proposed legislation being

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the-
I think the committee will be glad to see-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On behalf of the consumers of my riding, and on behalf of those who regard the Liberals as a low tariff party, I object to the increase in the tariff on mixed fruits. Not only do I object to the increase, I object to the behaviour of the government in connection with this matter over the past several years. It is a long story, which is pretty well known to the minister and those opposite, and I shall not go into the details. I think the way in which a departmental ruling was made, which was overruled by the tariff board and which was pursued in one way or another until the government finally got its way, was something that should be called, not behaviour but misbehaviour.

I just want to make sure that some hon. members of this house-and I refer not only to socialist members but also to some Liberal members who have been ready to spring to arms and utter loud cries every time anything is said in this house about protecting the Canadian farmer or the Canadian workman against unfair competition -will take due note of the fact that here the government is taking a very proper and necessary step to protect the Canadian fruit grower against what has become an unfair form of competition.
It may be, as the hon. member for Lincoln has said, that the situation has arisen through a lack of foresight at the time this item was written and in not foreseeing that the time would come when there would be certain mixtures of fruit imported into this country. I do hope that due note will be taken by some hon. members whom I do not see in the house at the moment but who have been most vocal on this subject-I see the hon. member for Rosthern is present-of the fact that this government is now taking the step of proposing an increase in the tariff, doubling the tariff on this particular fruit mixture, for the purpose of protecting the Canadian fruit farmer against what is otherwise an unfair form of competition.

Having said that, may I ask a question about the extent of the proposed change. The mixture we are speaking about has been described by the hon. member for Lincoln as a fruit cocktail, and this is described in 106(d) as a "mixture containing peaches, pears or apricots". Why is pineapple not included in the mixture? We dealt with pineapple in a previous item which remains unchanged, but here the mixture is of peaches, pears or apricots. And cherries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

If the fruit cocktail has in fact in it peaches, pears or apricots, any one of them, it comes under the item referred to. It probably would have pineapple as well, but the fact that it does contain pineapple would not exclude it from the benefits of the item.
I have noted the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and I must say I do not feel that his remarks about the actions of the government in the past are warranted. I know he feels that the government should not raise this particular item from 1 to 2 cents, or whatever it is, but I would point out that this action has been taken after negotiations with the only other government that would be concerned, and it has met with their approval. Under the circumstances I think it is a proper action within the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
May I also answer one other remark of the hon. member for Eglinton. I do not think he is suggesting that back in 1946 or 1947, whichever it was, it should have been the duty of the officials of the Department of National Revenue to have foreseen the development of fruit cocktails in cans.
I made it quite clear that when I referred to lack of foresight I did not suggest that there was anything culpable about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I would hesitate to suggest that anything the minister says is not correct, but I think there have been judges, perhaps not of the calibre they should have been, who have been stupid enough to look only at the words of the item and not at what the minister has said in the house. I suggest most earnestly that it would be wise if a change were made. I am not going to suggest it tonight. As I say, there are judges who might be perverse enough not to follow what the Minister of Finance has said. They will look at the item and consider that their bible and not go beyond it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I wish to say just one word in answer to the minister. I do not blame him for not liking my criticism of what I referred to as government misbehaviour. In view of the minister's reply I think I should put this further brief statement on the record.
In the first instance the schedule was set up without any reference to mixed fruits, and the department ruled that therefore mixed fruits came under the "n.o.p." item. Later on the department took the liberty of making a change and saying that henceforth mixed fruits would be peaches and were therefore

dutiable at that rate. The matter was referred to the tariff board, which ruled that the government was wrong.
It seems to me that if the government were determined to increase the rate they should have brought the matter to parliament, but they went on and there were appeals by the government and by those on the other side to various courts until a final decision was given, with the result that the government had to make repayments running into millions of dollars.
I do not think that the government should play around with parliament in that way. I think this is one type of thing that goes on in relation to tariffs which is very bad. Virtually changes in the tariff are being made by administrative decision within the department. If changes are to be made in the tariff schedules, they should be made by bringing the matter before parliament. It is because I hold that view that I expressed the opinion I did a moment ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend has read the report of the tariff board on that particular item. It was referred to the tariff board by my predecessor, and before the committee carried out the recommendation of the tariff board they studied the whole question of ethylene glycol and its components.
May I ask this question, Mr. Chairman. Is the minister in agreement with the general prediction being made today that the result of this will be a higher price in Canada for antifreeze?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a great many things will enter into the cost of the various forms of antifreeze. I think my hon. friend knows that some forms of antifreeze have a very high content of alcohol, and some a fairly low content. There is good competition in this particular field in Canada. It may well be that my hon. friend will be able to buy the product at one place at $3.50, or whatever the current price is, and get something at $2.95 at another place. I am sure he can. It depends on how much he wants of a pure product when he pays the price at a gasoline station.
I realize that the moment this was announced someone predicted it would bring an increase in the price of antifreeze. I suppose that is the thought anyone has, when there is a change in the tariff, but I should point out that there are reductions in the tariff in the three items referred to here. I would not think that the increase in the one item would be sufficient to make any material difference in the price of antifreeze.

Mr. Chairman, let me put it this way. If, as a result of the increase in the tariff, the government find there are substantial increases in the prices of antifreeze in Canada, would they be prepared then to recommend that this tariff be reduced again? That is question 1.
The second question is this. The minister referred to the fact that there is a decrease in the tariff under item 207d, which is quite all right with me. But you will notice that ethylene glycol is the base which is used for the manufacture of antifreeze. It would appear to me that by placing a tariff against the base product and lowering the tariff on the finished product, antifreeze itself, we are going to be importing more antifreeze and preventing it from being manufactured here to the extent of the increase in the tariff on

the base product. Surely that is not the result the government wishes. I am sure the government would not wish to restrict or hamper in any way the manufacture of this product in Canada. Yet that would be the result of this tariff increase.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to exercise my rights as a member of this house. It is now 25 minutes to eleven, and I say it is an imposition on the good nature of the members of this house to carry on further at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure it is an imposition on the good nature of the members to have to spend extra hours like this on the work of the house. But this is the last item of the resolution, and if the resolution were carried tonight, the bill would be available for distribution and consideration before we have to take it up again.

On that question, Mr. Chairman, could we ask the hon. leader of the house if he would tell us what will be the business for tomorrow, so those of us who want to get prepared for that can so do and the rest can talk as long as they jolly well please, for the rest of the night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I for one promise not to say another word, and when the resolution is carried I shall announce the business.
Those who wish to speak may do so for as long as they like, but for those who do not wish to take part in this, can you tell us what the business will be for tomorrow?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the second resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, 1 still do not think the minister has satisfied the house on this point. I should like to ask him whether his attention was called to the report on the profits made on ethylene glycol. I am referring to the report made by the restrictive trade practices commission to the Minister of Justice only some 24 months ago, wherein a very high rate was mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, could I say one word. I think I am partly responsible for our sitting after ten o'clock. Though we did not make any promise, we acquiesced in the minister's proposal in the hope that we could get through quickly. Now it looks as though we are branching into a discussion that might go on indefinitely. If those who are asking questions are not prepared to let this go now and let the rest of the discussion come on the bill, then it seems to me the time has come when we might ask the minister to call it ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the consideration the house has given, and I would hope we could postpone any further questioning until this section of the bill is dealt with. I could answer my hon. friend immediately, though. He will recall that the price of antifreeze fell quite noticeably about two years ago, at the time to which he is referring. I am aware of the report he speaks of. If hon. members find it possible to leave further discussion of this until the bill is dealt with, I would appreciate it very much.

Resolution agreed to.
Resolutions 3 and 4 agreed to.
Resolutions reported, read the second time and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill No. 506, to amend the Customs Tariff.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall take third reading of the bill to amend the Canada Elections Act; then the resolution with respect to the Income Tax Act, the Railway Act and the Tariff Board Act; then second reading of the amendment to the Criminal Code; then second reading of the bill to amend the Judges Act; then second reading of the bill to amend the Transport Act. I understand that representations have been made and that my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has decided that this bill might
Customs Tariff
properly be referred to a committee. On that understanding I am hopeful that the debate will not be extended on second reading, so we could have the matter placed at once before a committee and could invite here certain persons who wish to make representations.
When that business has been completed we shall perhaps ask the indulgence of the house to revert to the amendments to the Income Tax Act, the Railway Act and the Tariff Board Act in order to take second reading, if that is found possible after having heard the explanation at the committee stage. Then we shall move to go into supply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Silence now does not necessarily mean consent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. Then as I say, we will move to go into supply and if we get into supply we shall take the estimates of the Department of Fisheries.
May I ask the minister whether he is now in a position to indicate what the business will be on Thursday and Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Consideration of the estimates of the Department of Fisheries first, and then those of the Department of Justice.
When is it intended to call the Department of National Defence again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: At the moment there is no plan. I will see what arrangements can be made.
It being forty-five minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday. June 22, 1955
